title: Columnstore for a Telemetry Roll-Up
description: A per-sensor roll-up over millions of rows scans the rowstore in row mode; a nonclustered columnstore index aggregates it in batch mode. Why it matters: telemetry and IoT-style data (huge row counts, simple aggregates) is an increasingly common workload shape, and columnstore is the standard modern answer for it.
narrative:
## Scenario
An analytics query averages readings per sensor over 800,000 telemetry rows. On the rowstore clustered index it reads the entire table, row by row, every time.

## Why it's slow
The clustered index is **row-oriented**: to average one column it still pulls whole rows through the engine, one at a time (row mode). For a scan-everything aggregation, that's a lot of wasted I/O and CPU — rowstore is built for point lookups and small ranges, not for crunching a whole column.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** feeding a hash aggregate, touching the full table in row mode.
- An analytical query (`SUM`/`AVG`/`COUNT ... GROUP BY`) over a large table.

## The concept
Add a **nonclustered columnstore index** on the aggregated columns. Columnstore stores data by column in compressed segments and processes it in **batch mode** (hundreds of rows per CPU step), so a per-sensor average scans far less data far faster. Nonclustered columnstore lets the same table keep serving OLTP lookups on the rowstore while analytics use the columnstore — the HTAP pattern.
hints: The rowstore clustered index is scanned in row mode to aggregate a whole column -- the wrong storage for analytics.
A columnstore index stores data by column and processes it in batch mode, ideal for SUM/AVG/COUNT over big tables.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX NCCI_Measurements ON Measurements(SensorId, Reading); then re-run.
